title: At what noise level does EU law require hearing protection training?
seoTitle: EU noise at work directive training
description: When Directive 2003/10/EC requires noise training (80 dB(A) lower action value), the eight Article 8 topics, hearing protector rules, and audit evidence.
shortAnswer: Under the EU Noise at Work Directive (Directive 2003/10/EC), training becomes mandatory once a worker's daily noise exposure reaches the lower exposure action value of 80 dB(A) or a peak sound pressure of 112 Pa. Article 8 then requires information and training on eight topics, including the nature of noise risks, the exposure values, the employer's measurement results, correct use of hearing protectors, how to detect and report hearing damage, health surveillance rights, and safe working practices.
keyTakeaways: The training trigger is the lower exposure action value: a daily noise exposure level of 80 dB(A) or a peak sound pressure of 112 Pa.
Article 8 of Directive 2003/10/EC lists eight training topics, from the nature of the risk to safe working practices.
Hearing protectors must be made available above 80 dB(A) and used at or above 85 dB(A); the 87 dB(A) limit value takes their attenuation into account.
Workers above 85 dB(A) have a right to a hearing check, and preventive audiometry must be available above 80 dB(A) where the assessment indicates a health risk.
Member States had to transpose the directive before February 15, 2006, with extra time for the music and entertainment sectors and for applying the limit value to seagoing personnel.
jurisdiction: European Union (applied through each Member State's national law)
regulator: National labor inspectorates enforce the transposing laws; the European Commission monitors transposition; the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA) publishes guidance
appliesTo: Employers whose workers are or are likely to be exposed to noise as a result of their work
Workers exposed at or above 80 dB(A) daily or 112 Pa peak, and their representatives
Workers in the music and entertainment sectors, covered by national codes of conduct
Supervisors who enforce hearing protection and marked high noise areas

sections.heading: What is the EU Noise at Work Directive?

blocks.text: The Noise at Work Directive is [Directive 2003/10/EC](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02003L0010-20190726) of February 6, 2003, which sets minimum requirements for protecting workers from risks arising from exposure to noise, "in particular the risk to hearing". It is the seventeenth individual directive under the [OSH Framework Directive](/regulations/eu-osh-framework-directive-training), which continues to apply in full. It repealed the earlier noise directive, 86/188/EEC.

Article 17 required Member States to bring national laws into force before February 15, 2006. Member States could take up to two more years for the music and entertainment sectors, to allow a code of conduct to be drawn up, and up to five more years to apply the exposure limit rule in Article 7 to personnel on board seagoing vessels. As at November 2026 all of those transitional periods have long expired, and the consolidated text dated July 26, 2019 is current.

sections.heading: What are the exposure values that trigger training and protection?

blocks.text: Article 3 sets three tiers, each with a daily noise exposure level (L EX,8h) and a peak sound pressure. Training under Article 8 is triggered at the lowest tier.

blocks.text: Article 3(2) is a point training must get right: the limit value accounts for the attenuation provided by the worker's hearing protectors, but the action values "shall not take account of the effect of any such protectors". A worker who wears protectors in an 86 dB(A) area is still above the upper action value and still needs the training, the protectors, and the hearing check entitlement.

sections.heading: What must noise training cover under Article 8?

blocks.text: Article 8 requires the employer to ensure that workers exposed at or above the lower exposure action values, and/or their representatives, receive information and training on risks from noise concerning, in particular, eight topics:

items: the measures taken to implement the directive to eliminate or reduce noise risks, including the circumstances in which the measures apply
the exposure limit values and exposure action values in Article 3
the results of the assessment and measurement of noise under Article 4, "together with an explanation of their significance and potential risks"
the correct use of hearing protectors
why and how to detect and report signs of hearing damage
the circumstances in which workers are entitled to health surveillance and its purpose
safe working practices to minimize exposure to noise

blocks.text: Topic (d) means generic content is not enough. Each worker needs to know the measured levels for their own area or task and what those numbers mean for them. Topic (f) turns the worker into an early warning system, so training should cover symptoms such as ringing in the ears or muffled hearing after a shift, and name the reporting route.

Training also appears among the prevention measures. Article 5(1)(d) lists "adequate information and training to instruct workers to use work equipment correctly in order to reduce their exposure to noise to a minimum" as one of the ways to reduce risk at source.

sections.heading: How do hearing protector and health surveillance rules affect the training?

blocks.text: Hearing protector training must cover selection, fit, and consistent wear, because the employer is responsible for checking that protectors actually work. Article 6(1)(c) requires protectors to be selected to eliminate or minimize the risk to hearing, and Article 6(2) requires the employer to "make every effort to ensure the wearing of hearing protectors" and to check the effectiveness of the measures.

Under Article 10(2), a worker whose exposure exceeds the upper action value has the right to a hearing check by a doctor or a suitably qualified person under a doctor's responsibility. Article 10(4) requires the employer to review the risk assessment and the control measures if surveillance finds noise induced hearing damage, which in practice often leads to retraining. Article 9 requires consultation with workers or their representatives on the choice of hearing protectors, a step that also improves acceptance.

blocks.text: Linking each training record to the exposure data that triggered it makes it easy to show who needed training and why. That linkage is the core of [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations).

sections.heading: Are there special rules for music, entertainment, or combined exposures?

blocks.text: Yes. Article 14 requires Member States, in consultation with the social partners, to draw up a code of conduct with practical guidelines to help workers and employers in the music and entertainment sectors meet their obligations, so training in those sectors should reflect the national code.

Article 4(6)(d) requires the risk assessment to consider, as far as technically achievable, interactions between noise and work related ototoxic substances, and between noise and vibration. Where those interactions exist, noise training should be coordinated with chemical training under the [Chemical Agents Directive](/regulations/eu-chemical-agents-directive-worker-training). Article 4(6)(e) adds indirect effects from noise masking warning signals. EU-OSHA's [summary of Directive 2003/10/EC](https://osha.europa.eu/en/legislation/directives/82) also points to the Commission's non binding guide to good practice for applying the directive.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models the eight Article 8 topics as concepts with assessment points and links them to the measured exposure for each area and role. When new measurements move a role across an action value, the people who need training, and the specific concepts they need, can be identified from those links.

faqs.q: Do workers below 80 dB(A) need noise training?
faqs.a: Article 8 of Directive 2003/10/EC applies from the lower exposure action value (80 dB(A) or 112 Pa peak). Below it, the Framework Directive's general information and training duties still apply, and national law may set lower thresholds, so check the transposing act.

faqs.q: How often must noise training be repeated?
faqs.a: The directive sets no fixed interval. Topic (d) requires training on the results of the employer's assessment and measurement, so new measurements, new equipment, or changed control measures should trigger an update. Many organizations also set a periodic refresh under their own risk assessment.

faqs.q: Do hearing protectors count when deciding whether training is required?
faqs.a: No. Article 3(2) says the exposure action values do not take account of hearing protectors. Only the 87 dB(A) exposure limit value is assessed with the attenuation of the protectors worn, so a protected worker can still be above an action value.

faqs.q: Who can measure noise for the assessment?
faqs.a: Article 4(4) requires assessment and measurement to be planned and carried out by competent services at suitable intervals, referring to Article 7 of the Framework Directive on competent services or persons. The data must be preserved so it can be consulted later.

Article 8: information and training for workers at or above the lower exposure action values on topics (a) to (h)

Article 6(1)(a) to (c) protectors available above lower action values, used at or above upper action values, selected to eliminate or minimize risk; Article 6(2) employer makes every effort to ensure wearing and checks effectiveness; Article 5(1)(d) training to use work equipment correctly; Article 5(2) and (3) program of measures, signs and restricted access above upper action values

Article 10(2) right to hearing check above upper action values, preventive audiometry above lower action values where assessment indicates risk; Article 10(4) review of assessment on hearing damage; Article 9 consultation on choice of protectors; Article 4(4) competent services, data preserved; Article 4(6)(d) ototoxic substances and vibration
